title: When to back a decision
header_line: Jose's analysis of a book we are still naming. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: When a leader makes a drastic decision, how do you decide whether to back it?

A student said: this is the mentality of layoffs. I've got to sacrifice some to save the greater good. The idea is that if I allow a bloated company to happen, the whole company goes down. It's a big thing for fairly young people to tackle, and the main thing they have going for them is faith, belief and loyalty.

Another said: as the team members who remain after such a drastic cut, you think: I feel pretty lucky to still be here. If they made that decision, you're part of the elite, and you're here for a reason.
Jose asked: when do you not trust this situation? When do you say: this is not the right decision? And when do you say: he deserves my faith? That is a pretty tough question.

A student said: you have to determine for yourself what you value, what you believe is good. You can ask other people you trust, and in the end you do what you feel is right in your gut. Another said: look at other companies that were in similar spots.
A student said: they have seen the track record. Even if his decisions don't always make sense up front, they always end up playing out for the betterment of the company. That helps with the faith.

Jose said: that is where I am going. Let's study his decision process, what he has done in the past, the patterns, the outcomes. Is he one out of ten? Seven out of ten? What is the evidence his decisions lead to successful outcomes?

Just because a chief executive is paid fifty million dollars a year doesn't necessarily mean he is making good decisions, Jose said. A student said: how many at bats has he had? Jose said: I've been in a situation where the last eight or nine decisions a person made really hurt the company. Something in his decision process has changed.

Jose said that for the young people it comes down to kind of blind faith: this person has done it so far with the other companies. But if you are a veteran you will go into a company and look at what decisions have worked for this person.

A student said: it can be an advantage to be youthful and idealistic and not as jaded. If I see massive layoffs, I start with: how did they get to the point where they had to have them? What decision did they make or not make? Is it a failure of leadership?

Jose set another case: you are in a venture firm and a young chief executive is raising two hundred million. You have to gauge whether the person is making the right decisions. A student said: you have no track record to run with.
What is your evidence that the person you back decides well?

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write a leader whose hard decision you had to back.
Write what you used to decide.
Write the evidence of their track record.
Write the sign that would make you stop trusting them.
Write how you would gauge a person who has no track record.

check.q: What did Jose say to study about a leader?
choices: His decision process, patterns and outcomes

check.q: What did a student ask about a leader's track record?
choices: How many at bats has he had?

check.q: What did a student say is a resource when deciding to trust?
choices: Your gut, trusted people, and similar companies

recap: Judge a leader by the pattern and the evidence of their decisions. Know what you value.
